items.test:
D23-059 (observe mode, polling frames) and D23-061 (AID registration, `requireDeviceUnlock`,
relay exposure) own the configuration checks — run them and reuse the rows; this item keeps only the
relay framing. Two questions. (a) Does the app register a `HostApduService` in the `payment` category and ask
to become the default NFC payment app — the shape that allows relaying live EMV transactions, with the
POS talking ISO 14443-4/EMV to the phone and the app forwarding APDUs over a C2 channel while a backend
crafts responses? (b) On Android 15+, does the app run logic in `processPollingFrames()` *before* the
user has consented to anything?
items.how:
```bash
grep -n 'HostApduService\|android.nfc.cardemulation' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml -A8
cat $DEC/apktool/res/xml/apduservice.xml 2>/dev/null
grep -rnE 'processCommandApdu|processPollingFrames|registerPollingLoopPatternFilterForService|setPreferredService|CardEmulation' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -A10
adb shell dumpsys nfc | grep -iE 'aid|default|payment|observe'
```
items.proof:
For (a): the registered AIDs from `apduservice.xml` plus a captured APDU exchange being
forwarded off-device. For (b): pre-consent code paths executing on a polling frame, shown in logcat
before any user interaction.
items.escalation: → D23 for the payment impact; → D15 for the C2 channel's backend.
items.ruled_out_when:
No `HostApduService` is registered, or the service's `processCommandApdu` refuses
every APDU until an in-app authenticated session exists (demonstrate with a reader before login).

items.title: BLE link content is readable by every app on the device
items.severity_note: High when the payload is a credential or an actuation command; Medium for telemetry
items.attacker: AM-04 local app with one common permission; AM-10 proximity for the replay
items.applies_to: any app using BLE. Android 12+ splits `BLUETOOTH_CONNECT`/`SCAN`/`ADVERTISE` — note which the eavesdropping app needs
items.maps_to: `developer.android.com/develop/connectivity/bluetooth/ble/ble-overview`, verbatim caution: "When a user pairs their device with another device using BLE, the data that's communicated between the two devices is accessible to **all** apps on the user's device. For this reason, if your app captures sensitive data, you should implement app-layer security to protect the privacy of that data"; MASWE-0026
items.skip_when: `adb -s "$SERIAL" shell 'for f in android.hardware.bluetooth_le; do pm has-feature $f >/dev/null && echo "$f=true" || echo "$f=false"; done'` prints `false` for BLE on the test device: record the row as `blocked (hardware: <feature> absent on <serial>)` — never `n/a` and never a negative; move it to a device that has the feature.
items.test:
Google documents the channel as device-wide readable. If the app's BLE protocol carries tokens,
health readings, door or vehicle commands, or firmware, and relies on BLE link-layer encryption rather
than app-layer crypto, then any other app on the phone can read it — no root, one common permission.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'connectGatt|BluetoothGatt|writeCharacteristic|readCharacteristic|setCharacteristicNotification|BluetoothGattServer|PERMISSION_(READ|WRITE)_ENCRYPTED|createBond' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -A8
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell setprop persist.bluetooth.btsnooplogmode full   # Android 9+; or Developer options > Enable Bluetooth HCI snoop log (the pre-9 `bluetooth_hci_log` setting is LEGACY)
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell 'svc bluetooth disable; sleep 2; svc bluetooth enable'   # the mode is read at stack start
# reproduce the app's flow, then collect the log (written to /data/misc/bluetooth/logs/, retrievable without root via bugreport)
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys bluetooth_manager | grep -iE 'snoop|bonded|GATT'
adb -s "$SERIAL" bugreport br.zip && unzip -o br.zip 'FS/data/misc/bluetooth/logs/btsnoop_hci.log' -d br/
# rooted: adb -s "$SERIAL" shell su -c 'cat /data/misc/bluetooth/logs/btsnoop_hci.log' > btsnoop_hci.log
wireshark br/FS/data/misc/bluetooth/logs/btsnoop_hci.log   # filter: btatt
```
items.proof:
The plaintext token, command or reading visible in a Wireshark ATT packet from the snoop log,
with the corresponding app action timestamped. The finding is "no app-layer confidentiality on a channel
the platform explicitly documents as device-wide readable" — quote the caution.
items.escalation:
Replay the captured command from a second phone → unauthorised actuation. → D12 if the
payload is key material; → D23 if it is a payment or unlock command.
items.ruled_out_when:
The ATT payloads are ciphertext under an app-layer key that is not itself derivable
from the APK (check D12), or the sensitive values never traverse the link. Show the captured packets as
the negative.

items.title: The app's own GATT server accepts writes from an unbonded peer
items.severity_note: Critical when the write can push firmware or a credential; High when it triggers an action, changes configuration, or feeds a parser
items.attacker: AM-10 proximity, no app installed on the victim's phone
items.applies_to: apps that expose a `BluetoothGattServer`. Android 16's improved bond-loss handling changes bond-removal UX but not this
items.maps_to: the BLE overview's app-layer-security requirement; MASWE-0018
items.skip_when: `adb -s "$SERIAL" shell 'for f in android.hardware.bluetooth_le; do pm has-feature $f >/dev/null && echo "$f=true" || echo "$f=false"; done'` prints `false` for BLE on the test device: record the row as `blocked (hardware: <feature> absent on <serial>)` — never `n/a` and never a negative; move it to a device that has the feature.
items.test:
Apps exposing a GATT server for companion pairing, file transfer or "connect your watch"
frequently register characteristics with `PERMISSION_WRITE` rather than `PERMISSION_WRITE_ENCRYPTED` or
`_SIGNED`, so any nearby device can connect and write without bonding.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'BluetoothGattServer|addService|BluetoothGattCharacteristic\(|PERMISSION_WRITE|PERMISSION_WRITE_ENCRYPTED|PROPERTY_WRITE|onCharacteristicWriteRequest|getBondState|BOND_BONDED' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -A10
```
The vulnerable shape is `onCharacteristicWriteRequest(...)` acting on `value` with no
`device.getBondState() == BOND_BONDED` check and no app-layer authentication. From a second machine:
```bash
bluetoothctl scan on           # find the advertised name/UUID
bluetoothctl connect <MAC>     # then interactively: menu gatt / select-attribute <uuid> / write "0x01 0x02"   (gatttool is deprecated in BlueZ 5 and not built by default)
python3 - <<'PY'               # or bleak (pip install bleak), the same write without pairing
import asyncio
from bleak import BleakClient
async def main():
    async with BleakClient("<MAC>") as c:
        await c.write_gatt_char("<uuid>", bytes([0x01, 0x02]), response=True)
asyncio.run(main())
PY
# or: nRF Connect on a second phone, write the characteristic
```
items.proof:
The app reacting to a write from an unbonded peer — logcat from the target app plus the
`bluetoothctl`/`bleak` or nRF transcript showing no pairing occurred.
items.escalation:
→ D16 if the written bytes reach native code; → D17 if they are a firmware image; →
D25-040 for the firmware-integrity question.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every writable characteristic is declared `PERMISSION_WRITE_ENCRYPTED` or `_SIGNED`,
or `onCharacteristicWriteRequest` returns `GATT_INSUFFICIENT_AUTHENTICATION` for an unbonded device —
show the refusal in the `bluetoothctl`/`bleak` transcript.

items.title: CompanionDeviceManager association with an attacker-controlled device, and `removeBond()`
items.severity_note: High when the association grants a persistent background channel into a privileged code path, or when `removeBond()` is reachable from an exported component; Medium for the association alone (it needs a tap in the picker)
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.exposed_sensitive_android_intent` (**VARIES**, CWE-927) for the exported `removeBond()` path; rated by the reached impact
items.attacker: AM-10 proximity; AM-03 for the exported-component variant
items.applies_to: apps using CDM; `CompanionDeviceManager#removeBond(int)` is Android 16+
items.maps_to: `developer.android.com/about/versions/16/behavior-changes-16` (`CompanionDeviceManager#removeBond(int)`; monitor `BluetoothDevice#ACTION_BOND_STATE_CHANGED`); `developer.android.com/about/versions/16/behavior-changes-all` — "Companion apps no longer notified of discovery timeouts": companion apps now receive `RESULT_USER_REJECTED` instead of `RESULT_DISCOVERY_TIMEOUT`, which changes the error handling your PoC will see on API 36+
items.test:
`CompanionDeviceManager.associate()` presents a picker of nearby devices filtered by name, MAC
or UUID pattern. A spoofed advertiser matching the filter appears in that picker; a user who taps it
grants an association, after which the app may auto-connect, sync and — with
`REQUEST_COMPANION_RUN_IN_BACKGROUND` — act on the attacker device's data indefinitely. Separately,
check whether the app exposes `removeBond()` through an exported component, which lets an unprivileged
app force a companion peripheral to unpair.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'CompanionDeviceManager|AssociationRequest|BluetoothLeDeviceFilter|BluetoothDeviceFilter|WifiDeviceFilter|setNamePattern|REQUEST_COMPANION|removeBond' \
     $DEC/jadx/sources/ $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml -A8
adb shell dumpsys companiondevice
adb shell dumpsys companiondevice | grep -A5 com.target.app
```
Then advertise from a second device with a name matching the app's `setNamePattern` regex and complete
the association. For the `removeBond()` path, drive the exported component from a zero-permission app.
items.proof:
`dumpsys companiondevice` listing your spoofed device as associated with the target package,
followed by the app syncing or acting on data you supplied. For `removeBond()`: the companion device
unpairing on command from the PoC app, with `ACTION_BOND_STATE_CHANGED` in the log.
items.escalation:
→ D25-057/D25-058 with a durable, user-blessed channel. Forced unpairing of a lock, a
key fob or a medical device either denies service or forces a re-pair the attacker can intercept.
items.ruled_out_when:
The association request uses a `BluetoothDeviceFilter` pinned to a MAC address or a
service UUID the attacker cannot claim, **and** no exported component reaches `removeBond()`. An
over-broad name pattern (`.*` or a common prefix) is itself worth calling out even when nothing else
holds.

items.title: Scanner acting on `Barcode.getWifi()` — joining an attacker-chosen network on a scan
items.severity_note: High when the app has any unpinned host; Medium otherwise
items.vrt: `insecure_data_transport.cleartext_transmission_of_sensitive_data` (**VARIES**, CWE-319 — rated on what the network position then reaches) via the network position; the rated finding is whatever the MitM then reaches
items.attacker: AM-02 remote one click (the user scans a sticker); then AM-06 network attacker
items.applies_to: apps whose scanner enables the Wi-Fi barcode format
items.maps_to: `developers.google.com/ml-kit/vision/barcode-scanning/android` — `Barcode.getWifi()`, `getValueType()`; the page gives no validation guidance
items.test:
A scanner that supports the Wi-Fi barcode type (`WIFI:T:WPA;S:…;P:…;;`) can offer to join a
network from a scanned code. The attacker chooses the SSID and PSK and therefore the DNS and the
gateway — a scan becomes a network-position attack delivered by a sticker.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'getWifi\(\)|Barcode\.TYPE_WIFI|WifiNetworkSuggestion|WifiNetworkSpecifier|addNetwork|enableNetwork|WifiManager' $DEC/jadx/sources
qrencode -o wifi.png 'WIFI:T:WPA;S:AttackerAP;P:Passw0rd123;;'
# scan it, then:
adb shell dumpsys wifi | grep -iE 'SSID|Suggestion'
```
items.proof:
The device joining, or offering a one-tap join to, the attacker's SSID directly from the scan
— screen-record the scan-to-join, then show the app's subsequent traffic traversing the attacker's
gateway.
items.escalation:
Network position plus any unpinned host is the D14 MitM chain with the hardest part
(getting the position) solved by the app itself.
items.ruled_out_when:
The scanner restricts `getValueType()` to the formats the feature needs, or the app
never calls a Wi-Fi join API with scanned values. Check `setBarcodeFormats()` — an unrestricted scanner
that nonetheless ignores `TYPE_WIFI` in its handler is a true negative; say which.

items.title: Android Auto `CarAppService` with `ALLOW_ALL_HOSTS_VALIDATOR`
items.severity_note: High
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (**VARIES**, CWE-269); `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (**VARIES**) for the rendered account data
items.applies_to: any app shipping an Android for Cars integration (categories `androidx.car.app.category.NAVIGATION` / `.POI` / `.IOT` / `.WEATHER`)
items.maps_to: `developer.android.com/training/cars/apps` — the docs name `createHostValidator()` and `HostValidator.ALLOW_ALL_HOSTS_VALIDATOR` and explicitly warn to validate the binding host; MASWE-0018; How owner: D06-054
items.test:
The `CarAppService` is exported by necessity so the car host can bind it. The library's gate
deciding *which* host may bind is `createHostValidator()`. Shipping
`HostValidator.ALLOW_ALL_HOSTS_VALIDATOR` means any app on the phone can bind and drive the car session
— a surface no phone-app checklist covers, and one that renders account data with no phone UI and no
lock-screen involvement.
items.how:
Run D06-054 — it owns the `createHostValidator()` grep and the bind-from-an-unprivileged-app
PoC; reuse its row. This chapter adds only the scope note: the car surface renders account data with no
phone UI and no lock-screen involvement, so route the finding to the programme that owns the Auto
integration and rate the rendered data, not the bind.
items.proof:
As D06-054 (the car-session lifecycle logs with your package as the client, and the template
contents captured in the bind callback).
items.escalation:
Session data read → account enumeration; command injection into navigation. Join with
D25-063: the car surface's endpoints are a second, weaker client.
items.ruled_out_when:
`createHostValidator()` returns a validator built with `addAllowedHosts()` pinned to
the Google host package and signature, or the service is not exported. Show the bind attempt being
refused, not just the source line.

items.title: Wear OS `WearableListenerService` dispatching on path with no node or capability check
items.severity_note: Critical if a path puts the phone app into an authenticated state; High to Medium otherwise
items.attacker: AM-03 (an app that can reach the Data Layer) / AM-10 (a paired attacker node)
items.applies_to: any app with a Wear OS companion. The Data Layer is Android-phone-only, so the path set is often *less* tested than the main API
items.maps_to: `developer.android.com/training/wearables/data/data-layer` and `.../data/messages` (`DataClient`, `MessageClient`, `WearableListenerService`, `sendMessage(nodeId, path, data)`); MASWE-0018, MASWE-0032; CVE-2025-12080 (intent abuse in Google Messages for Wear OS, patched May 2025) as evidence the form factor is a live surface; How owner: D06-055
items.test:
The Wear Data Layer delivers `DataItem`s and messages addressed by **path** (`/sync`, `/auth`,
`/logout`). The receiving service is exported so Google Play services can bind it. Test whether
`onMessageReceived` / `onDataChanged` dispatches on path alone with no `getSourceNodeId()` comparison
against a known, capability-verified node.
items.how:
Run D06-055 — it owns the path/`getSourceNodeId()` greps and the attacker-node delivery; reuse
its row. This chapter adds only the scope note: the watch is a second device, so the paired-node attacker
(AM-10) and the programme's wearable scope decide where the report goes; enumerate every `pathPrefix`
as the channel's undocumented API.
items.proof:
As D06-055 (a path-only dispatch with no node comparison, then the phone app acting on
attacker-chosen bytes delivered on that path).
items.escalation:
A trusted-by-path "auth complete" message is a direct authentication bypass over a
channel nobody tested → D13. On Wear the surface widens further: activities, foreground services (with
`FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK`), Tiles and Complications can all fire the same payload — exercise all four.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every handler compares `getSourceNodeId()` against a node obtained from
`CapabilityClient` for the app's own capability, and rejects unknown nodes. Show the rejection path.

items.title: The companion-surface API is a second, weaker client
items.severity_note: Critical (BOLA on a companion-only endpoint)
items.attacker: AM-05 another user of the same app
items.applies_to: apps with Wear, Auto, TV, widget or Tile companions
items.maps_to: the shadow-API method from the bug-hunting corpus: a mobile client's hardcoded backend calls are frequently an *older* API version than the current web app uses, with weaker auth, weaker rate limits, weaker validation and more field exposure. **Diff behaviourally, not by response shape. A version difference alone is Informational; the weakened control is the finding**
items.test:
Wear, Auto, TV and widget code paths frequently call *different* endpoints, or the same
endpoints with a different client id or scope, and were built by a smaller team under time pressure.
Extract those endpoints specifically and test them for the authorisation bugs already fixed on the
phone client.
items.how:
```bash
# endpoints referenced only by companion code
grep -rnE 'https?://[a-zA-Z0-9./_-]+' $DEC/jadx/sources/ | grep -iE 'wear|watch|auto|car|tv|widget|tile|glance' | sort -u > companion-hosts.txt
wc -l companion-hosts.txt          # count, per the shell-loop ban
# diff against the phone client's endpoint set
comm -23 <(sort -u companion-hosts.txt) <(sort -u phone-hosts.txt)
```
Then diff four security-relevant behaviours for the **same operation** across the phone path and the
companion path: auth strength (does the companion path accept no token, an expired token, or a
lower-privilege token the phone path rejects?), rate limiting (burst both; a missing 429 means
throttling was never applied to the companion path), input validation (same oversized or injected
payload to both), field exposure (does the companion response carry internal ids or PII the phone
response redacts?). Replay each with a low-privilege token and with another user's object id.
items.proof:
A 200 with another user's data from a companion-only endpoint that the phone endpoint rejects
with 403 — the status-code delta between the two paths, with both requests side by side and both
bodies diffed.
items.escalation: → D15 for the full authorisation surface on the newly found path.
items.ruled_out_when:
The companion paths are byte-identical to the phone paths in auth handling,
throttling and field set across all four behavioural axes. A different *URL* with identical behaviour is
Informational — do not file it.

items.title: Instant-App reachability and the endpoints a retired instant experience left live
items.severity_note: Medium to High, depending on what the endpoint returns
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.idor.view_sensitive_information_iterable_object_identifiers` (**P3**) or higher depending on the data; `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (**VARIES**)
items.attacker: AM-01 remote no interaction (for the live endpoints); AM-02 for the browser-triggered client path
items.applies_to: **LEGACY client, live server.** Google Play Instant is discontinued — as of December 2025 instant apps cannot be published and the Play services Instant APIs stop working. Any app that ever shipped an instant experience
items.maps_to: `developer.android.com/topic/google-play-instant/overview` (discontinuation timeline; `InstantApps.isInstantApp()`; the restricted API and permission subset); H1 #258460 (Quora) — the researcher's own published correction is the caution to heed: "services can be accessed by Instant Apps only in case when `android:visibleToInstantApps` flag is enabled"
items.test:
Two halves. (a) **Reachability discipline:** do not claim browser-triggerable Instant-App reach
for a component without checking `android:visibleToInstantApps` — this is a documented correction a
researcher had to publish about his own report. (b) **Live server exposure:** instant experiences were
built permission-light and often unauthenticated because instant apps could only use a subset of APIs
and permissions. Those endpoints frequently remain deployed long after the client is dead.
items.how:
```bash
grep -n 'visibleToInstantApps' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -rnE 'InstantApps|isInstantApp|dist:instant|dist:module|targetSandboxVersion' $DEC/jadx/sources/ $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -rnE 'instant|/i/|/lite/|guest' $DEC/jadx/sources/ | grep -iE 'http' | sort -u
# the deep links that used to launch the instant experience usually still resolve
grep -nE 'android:host=|android:pathPrefix=' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml | sort -u
adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d 'https://<host>/<instant-era-path>'
```
Then probe the discovered server paths unauthenticated.
items.escalation:
→ D15 for the endpoint's authorisation surface; → D09 for the deep-link handler. Almost
nobody checks this now that the client side is dead, which is precisely why it is worth ten minutes.
items.ruled_out_when:
The merged manifest carries no `dist:instant`, no `InstantApps` reference and no
`visibleToInstantApps`, and no instant-flavoured host appears in the host inventory. For the
reachability half: absence of `visibleToInstantApps="true"` on a service is the negative — state it
rather than claiming browser reach.

items.title: Enumerate every instance of the app that exists on the device
items.severity_note: Support (it converts D13 device-binding and D23 entitlement items from "unverified" to "demonstrated")
items.applies_to: Android 5+ for multi-user; Android 15+ for Private Space; OEM clone features vary
items.maps_to: `developer.android.com/about/versions/15/features#private-space` — "The private space uses a separate user profile", "Apps in the private space are installed as separate copies from any apps in the main space", and the explicit compatibility warning about apps "with work profile logic that assume any installed copies of their app that aren't in the main profile are in the work profile"; How owner: D01-052
items.test:
Every checklist assumes one install per device. On a real device the app may exist as user 0, a
work profile (user 10+), a Private Space profile, an OEM dual-app/clone instance, and a guest-user
instance. Each has its own data directory, its own FCM token and its own session — so any device-binding
or entitlement scheme that counts installs is wrong.
items.how:
Run D01-052 — it owns the enumeration (`pm list users`, `pm list packages --user all`, per-user
data directories, OEM clone ids); reuse its row. This chapter adds only what the enumeration feeds:
the reach tests in D25-066/067 and the device-demographic note (which OEM clone features the client's
fleet actually ships).
items.proof:
As D01-052 (two live data directories for the same package under different user ids, side by
side).
items.escalation:
Feeds D11 (cross-user data), D13 (device binding), D23 (trial and entitlement
duplication), and D25-066 (the reach tests).
items.ruled_out_when:
`pm list users` shows only user 0 and the OEM provides no clone feature on this
model. Record which OEM features you checked — the answer is model-specific.

items.title: Cross-user provider read and cross-user service bind
items.severity_note: High (cross-user data access is an explicitly bought impact class)
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.idor.modify_view_sensitive_information_iterable_object_identifiers` (**P1**) where it returns another user's records; `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (**VARIES**) otherwise
items.attacker: AM-05 another user of the same device
items.applies_to: Android 5+ multi-user; Private Space Android 15+
items.maps_to: Android & Google Devices in-scope impact, verbatim: "**Multi-User & Private Space:** Cross-user sensitive data access, or unlocking Private Space without the designated lock factor"; Samsung High: "Bypass Operating System protections including access memory or file contents across application, user, or profile boundaries"; How owners for the per-component tests: D07-011, D06-023 (this item keeps the crossing routes)
items.test:
D07-011 (provider from a second user / locked Private Space) and D06-023 (caller check never
compares the user id) own the per-component tests; this item adds the crossing **routes**. Everything in
every checklist binds and queries from user 0. A work profile, Private Space or OEM clone instance runs
as a different UID with a different data directory — and a service that guards on `getCallingUid()` or
on a same-signature check passes trivially for a *clone of the same app*. A plain app cannot resolve
another user's provider or bind its service without `INTERACT_ACROSS_USERS*` — which `adb shell` holds,
so every shell `--user` success is a false positive. The routes to test are: (1) a clone/work instance
in the SAME profile group reached through connected apps (D25-082) or `CrossProfileApps`; (2) a
preinstalled target with `android:singleUser="true"` services or an `INTERACT_ACROSS_USERS*` holder
acting as deputy; (3) user-shared storage (`/storage/emulated/<id>` on OEM clones, MediaStore); (4) a
backend identity keyed by device id rather than account.
items.how:
```bash
UID2=$(adb -s "$SERIAL" shell pm create-user gapuser | tr -d '\r' | grep -oE '[0-9]+$')   # never assume 10 (10 is usually the work profile)
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell am switch-user $UID2
adb -s "$SERIAL" install --user $UID2 probe.apk     # host path; a managed/private profile with DISALLOW_DEBUGGING_FEATURES needs `pm install-existing --user <id> com.probe` or the DPC test app
# the probe (NOT shell) queries content://0@com.target.app.provider/data and binds the service -> expect SecurityException naming INTERACT_ACROSS_USERS
# shell is the DISCOVERY tool only: proves the data exists, not reachability
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell content query --user 0 --uri content://com.target.app.provider/data
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys activity services com.target.app | grep -E 'user|clientUid|ConnectionRecord'
# the guard itself
grep -rnE 'getCallingUid|getCallingPackage|checkSignatures|getPackagesForUid|singleUser|INTERACT_ACROSS_USERS' $DEC/jadx/sources/ $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml -A6
```
The specific defect to look for: a guard that checks the UID or the signature but never compares
`UserHandle.getUserId(uid)`. Also test the file form: `file:///data/user/$UID2/com.target.app/…`.
items.proof:
The probe's result from user B with its uid in `dumpsys activity services` / the provider's
log — never a `--user` shell call. Screenshot `pm list users` and the dumpsys together. A
`Permission Denial … requires android.permission.INTERACT_ACROSS_USERS_FULL` for the probe is also a
reportable data point — it is the negative.
items.escalation:
→ D11 cross-user data read → D23 entitlement duplication → D15 if the rows contain
server object ids you can then enumerate.
items.ruled_out_when:
The probe gets `Permission Denial … INTERACT_ACROSS_USERS_FULL` for both query and
bind **and** routes 1–4 above were each tested, including the clone/work-profile variant (same profile
group, different UID), which is the case that most often crosses when a plain second user does not. By default a second user cannot see user 0's
packages — prove whether your call actually crossed rather than assuming it did.

items.title: Private Space boundary (Android 15)
items.severity_note: High
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.idor.modify_view_sensitive_information_iterable_object_identifiers` (**P1**) where data crosses; `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (**P1**) for unlocking without the designated factor
items.applies_to: Android 15+
items.maps_to: `developer.android.com/about/versions/15/behavior-changes-all` (private space as a separate user profile; launcher requirements `ROLE_HOME`, `ACCESS_HIDDEN_PROFILES`, `getLauncherUserInfo()`, `requestQuietModeEnabled()`, `ACTION_PROFILE_AVAILABLE`/`ACTION_PROFILE_UNAVAILABLE`; app stores must declare `android.intent.category.APP_MARKET`); `developer.android.com/about/versions/15/features`
items.test:
Private space installs apps into a separate user profile that is hidden when locked. Two
consequences: an app that assumes "another install of me must be in a work profile" mis-handles private
space, and data isolation between the private-space copy and the main copy must hold.
items.how:
```bash
adb shell pm list users
adb shell pm list packages --user <privateSpaceUserId> | grep com.target.app
adb shell am start --user <privateSpaceUserId> -n com.target.app/.MainActivity
grep -rn 'ACCESS_HIDDEN_PROFILES\|getLauncherUserInfo\|requestQuietModeEnabled\|ACTION_PROFILE_AVAILABLE\|ACTION_PROFILE_UNAVAILABLE\|ROLE_HOME' $DEC/jadx/sources/ $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
# then lock the private space and retry - apps there should be stopped
adb shell am get-current-user
```
items.proof:
Data written by the private-space instance readable from the main-profile instance or vice
versa — via a shared external path, a cloud account keyed only by device id, or a content provider that
does not scope by user. Or the private-space instance still responding after the space is locked.
items.escalation:
→ D11/D20. The privacy boundary broken by the app's own storage or sync design is the
finding, not the platform's.
items.ruled_out_when:
The private-space copy's data lives only under `/data/user/<id>/`, the app's
server-side identity is per-account rather than per-device, and the instance is stopped when the space
is locked. Test all three.

items.title: Work-profile data crossing the profile boundary
items.severity_note: High in an enterprise-scoped engagement (DLP bypass); out of scope for a consumer app without a managed configuration in scope
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (**VARIES**, CWE-269); `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.for_internal_asset` (**P3**) for the leaked corporate data
items.applies_to: managed devices only — work profile API 21+, fully managed API 21+. Confirm the engagement includes an enrolled device
items.maps_to: community work-profile checklists on cross-profile clipboard, sharing, notifications and file mediation; `DISALLOW_CROSS_PROFILE_COPY_PASTE`
items.test:
In a managed setup, confirm the app does not leak work data into the personal profile via
clipboard, sharing intents, notifications, contacts or a shared account.
items.how:
```bash
adb shell dpm list-owners
adb shell pm list users
adb shell am start --user 10 -n com.target/.MainActivity
adb shell dumpsys device_policy | sed -n '/Profile/,/^$/p'
adb shell dumpsys package | grep -A10 'Cross-profile'
```
Then copy a work-profile secret to the clipboard and attempt to paste it in a personal-profile app;
share a work document to a personal app; check whether work notifications render in the personal
profile.
items.proof:
Work-profile content appearing in a personal-profile app — a screenshot of the paste, or the
personal app receiving the shared file — **against an explicitly configured restriction** such as
`DISALLOW_CROSS_PROFILE_COPY_PASTE`. Without the restriction configured, cross-profile sharing is
intended behaviour and not a finding.
items.escalation: Enterprise DLP bypass; combine with D07 provider access across users.
items.ruled_out_when:
The restriction is configured and the paste or share is refused. Note that many
items in the public work-profile checklists target the **MDM/EMM platform**, not the app — those belong
in the MDM vendor's scope and should be routed there rather than filed against the app.

items.title: App behaviour under a device-policy restriction it claims to honour
items.severity_note: Medium to High in an enterprise engagement
items.applies_to: managed devices only
items.maps_to: community MDM checklists on screen-capture, camera, backup and managed-configuration enforcement
items.test:
Apply the policy restrictions the target claims to support — screen capture disabled, camera
disabled, backup disabled, app restrictions via managed configuration — and confirm the app actually
honours them rather than silently proceeding.
items.how:
```bash
adb shell dpm set-profile-owner com.dpc/.Receiver          # on a test device
adb shell dumpsys device_policy | grep -iE 'screenCapture|camera|backup|restrictions'
adb shell am get-config
adb shell screencap /sdcard/t.png && adb pull /sdcard/t.png
```
Then attempt a screenshot, a camera use and a backup from inside the app.
items.proof:
A successful `screencap` while `setScreenCaptureDisabled(true)` is in force for the profile,
or the app writing a backup despite the restriction.
items.escalation: Enterprise policy bypass → D20 for the captured content, D11 for the backup contents.
items.ruled_out_when:
`screencap` returns a black frame or fails, the camera call throws, and the backup
is refused — with `dumpsys device_policy` in the same capture showing the restriction active.

items.title: Work-profile required-app replacement
items.severity_note: Critical
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (**VARIES**, CWE-269); `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (**P1**) where the replaced app holds the enterprise session
items.attacker: AM-11 physical unlocked (temporary access to enable Developer Options and USB debugging)
items.applies_to: Android Enterprise BYOD work profiles with required-app policies
items.maps_to: CVE-2023-21257 (the patch being bypassed — ADB sideloads blocked under `DISALLOW_INSTALL_APPS` / `DISALLOW_DEBUGGING_FEATURES`); HackTricks android-enterprise-work-profile-bypass
items.test:
An MDM that marks an app *required* for the work profile auto-installs it if missing.
Combined with Android Studio's "Install for all users" staging, that lets an attacker with brief
physical access replace any required work-profile app — after the CVE-2023-21257 patch.
items.how:
```bash
adb shell pm list users          # user 0 = Owner, user 10 = Work profile
adb install --user 10 legit.apk  # expected: SecurityException: Shell does not have permission to access user 10
```
Build the payload with the **same package name** and a much larger `versionCode`:
```gradle
android { namespace = "com.workday.workdroidapp"
  defaultConfig { applicationId = "com.workday.workdroidapp"
    versionCode = 900000004; versionName = "9000000004.0" } }
```
Deploy from Android Studio with *Deploy as instant app → Install for all users* (`INSTALL_ALL_USERS`).
The work-user install is denied, but the legitimate app is marked uninstalled and the staged APK stays
cached. Within roughly 1–10 minutes the MDM notices the required package is missing and the
work-profile Play client reinstalls it — choosing the locally staged build because it has the highest
`versionCode`.
items.proof:
The malicious build running inside the work profile under the genuine package name, reported
as compliant by the MDM. Record the MDM's compliance screen alongside `pm path --user 10`.
items.escalation:
Enterprise data theft plus persistence — the MDM reinstalls it whenever it is removed.
If the replaced package is mapped to a per-app VPN, the malicious build inherits the VPN profile and
reaches internal hosts directly.
items.ruled_out_when:
The device enforces `DISALLOW_INSTALL_UNKNOWN_SOURCES` and
`DISALLOW_DEBUGGING_FEATURES` such that Developer Options cannot be enabled at all, or the MDM pins the
required app to a signing certificate and refuses a higher `versionCode` with a different signer. Test
the signer check explicitly — `versionCode` precedence is the mechanism.

items.title: Device Policy Controller removal and enterprise-control bypass
items.severity_note: High
items.attacker: AM-11 physical unlocked; AM-03 where an app surface reaches the removal
items.applies_to: managed and enterprise deployments
items.maps_to: Android & Google Devices in-scope impact, verbatim: "**Enterprise Bypasses:** Unauthorized removal of the Device Policy Controller (DPC)" — explicitly named in-scope and rarely covered in public checklists
items.test:
Whether a managed device's DPC can be removed, or its policies neutered, without
authorisation — including through the app under test's own surfaces.
items.how:
```bash
adb shell dpm list-owners
adb shell dumpsys device_policy | head -40
adb shell pm list packages -d | grep -i dpc
# then attempt removal through the app surface under test, and through the OEM's own flows
adb shell dpm remove-active-admin com.dpc/.Receiver
```
items.proof:
`dpm list-owners` showing no owner after your action, with the previously enforced policies
no longer applied (re-run the D25-069 checks and show them now passing).
items.escalation: Full managed-device compromise; combine with D25-070 for persistence.
items.ruled_out_when:
`dpm remove-active-admin` is refused, `DISALLOW_REMOVE_MANAGED_PROFILE` is set, and
no app surface reaches `removeActiveAdmin` / `clearProfileOwner`. Grep the app for those calls before
concluding.

items.title: Kiosk, lock-task and screen-pinning escape from inside the app
items.severity_note: High in a kiosk engagement (the device *is* the security boundary); N/A otherwise
items.attacker: AM-11 physical unlocked (a member of the public at the kiosk)
items.applies_to: dedicated/COSU/kiosk deployments only; scope it explicitly
items.maps_to: VRT `insecure_os_firmware > kiosk_escape_or_breakout`; community COSU/lock-task checklists
items.test:
Where the app runs as a kiosk or is used under screen pinning, look for a path out — a WebView
that opens an external browser, a share sheet, a settings deep link, a file picker, a print dialog, or
a crash that drops to the launcher.
items.how:
```bash
adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep -i 'lockTask\|mLockTaskModeState'
# from inside the app: exercise every link, share button, file picker and error dialog
adb shell am start -a android.settings.SETTINGS
adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "https://x"
adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.GET_CONTENT -t '*/*'
```
items.proof:
Reaching Settings, a browser or the launcher from inside the pinned app — screen recording
with `mLockTaskModeState` shown before and after.
items.escalation:
Full device access from a public kiosk → D25-044 (developer settings) → D25-043 (adb) →
the whole device.
items.ruled_out_when:
`mLockTaskModeState` remains `LOCK_TASK_MODE_LOCKED` through every exit attempt and
the allow-list (`setLockTaskPackages`) contains only the kiosk app. Enumerate the allow-list — a
permitted browser or file-manager package is the escape.

items.title: OEM MDM and firmware layers (Knox, E-FOTA and equivalents), and the null-means-compliant trap
items.severity_note: Medium to High in an enterprise engagement; a bug in the OEM layer itself belongs to the **OEM's** VRP, not the app vendor's
items.applies_to: OEM-managed fleets; out of scope for a standard app engagement unless the app itself ships the integration
items.maps_to: community enterprise checklists on Knox Guard, Knox Platform for Enterprise, E-FOTA, enterprise firmware update abuse, and generic Android Enterprise / EMM / UEM bypasses
items.test:
Where the app relies on an OEM container or policy API, check whether its assumptions hold when
that layer is absent, stubbed or downgraded. The recurring defect is treating a `null` return from the
vendor API as "policy satisfied".
items.how:
```bash
adb shell getprop | grep -iE 'knox|oem|miui|emui|coloros|oneui'
adb shell pm list packages | grep -iE 'knox|enterprise|kme|efota'
grep -rn 'com.samsung.android.knox\|EnterpriseDeviceManager\|KnoxContainerManager' $DEC/jadx/sources -A10
```
Then run the app on a device where the OEM API is absent (a non-Samsung handset, or one with the Knox
packages disabled) and observe whether it proceeds with its normal security posture.
items.proof:
The app proceeding normally on a device where the OEM container API is stubbed or absent —
the code path where `null` is treated as success, plus the runtime behaviour.
items.escalation:
Enterprise fleet compromise; route platform bugs to the OEM programme and the
null-handling bug to the app vendor. They are two reports.
items.ruled_out_when:
The app fails closed when the OEM API is unavailable — it refuses to enter the
protected mode and says so in the UI. Show the refusal on a non-OEM device.

items.title: Device-admin or accessibility status obtainable without informed consent
items.severity_note: Critical when obtained without informed consent
items.applies_to: all
items.maps_to: TapTrap (USENIX Security 2025), which explicitly lists Device Administrator status — "enables remote device wipe" — among the reachable outcomes; MASWE-0070 / MASWE-0078 (inadequate awareness/consent for privacy-relevant actions)
items.test:
Whether the app's own flows, or a TapTrap-style animation attack against them, can result in
Device Administrator activation or an accessibility grant that the user did not understand they were
giving.
items.how:
```bash
grep -n 'BIND_DEVICE_ADMIN\|DeviceAdminReceiver\|BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml -A6
adb shell dpm list-owners
adb shell settings get secure enabled_accessibility_services
adb shell dumpsys device_policy | head -40
adb shell dumpsys accessibility
```
Then run the tested flow and check whether the admin or service is active afterwards.
items.proof:
`dpm list-owners` or `dumpsys device_policy` showing the admin activated as a result of the
tested flow, or `enabled_accessibility_services` naming the service — with a recording of the consent
UI the user actually saw.
items.escalation:
An enabled accessibility service reads and drives every app on the device — the
mechanism behind Android banking-trojan overlays. → D20 for what it can read, D13 for OTP interception,
D23 for automated confirmation. **From Android 13 (API 33) a sideloaded app cannot be granted
accessibility without the user passing through "Allow restricted settings"** — state the OS version
your PoC used and whether the app was Play-installed, or the severity will be argued down.
items.ruled_out_when:
The app declares neither `BIND_DEVICE_ADMIN` nor `BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE`, and
the consent UI in the tested flow is the platform's own unmodified dialog with no overlay or animation
covering it.

items.title: Mobile foothold as an enterprise pivot
items.severity_note: Critical
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.for_internal_asset` (**P3**) for the recovered credential; the demonstrated corporate access sets the real rating
items.applies_to: enterprise and BYOD apps
items.maps_to: the "From APK to Golden Ticket" write-up (Pierini & Trotta, 2017) as the canonical shape of a mobile foothold leading to domain compromise
items.test:
For an enterprise or BYOD app, assess whether compromising the app yields corporate
credentials, VPN profiles or certificates — and say so in the app report even when you cannot use them.
items.how:
After any D11 or D07 primitive, search the recovered data specifically:
```bash
rg -n -i 'BEGIN (RSA|EC|OPENSSH) PRIVATE KEY|\.p12|\.pfx|krb5|NTLM|\\\\[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\\|vpn|ipsec|ikev2|enrol|mdm_token' loot/
adb shell run-as com.target.app find . -name '*.p12' -o -name '*.pfx' -o -name '*.conf'
adb shell dumpsys connectivity | grep -i vpn
```
items.proof:
The recovered credential authenticating against a corporate service — **with the client's
written permission for that step**, recorded in the RoE. Without that permission, stop at the recovered
artefact and describe what it is for.
items.escalation:
Domain compromise is the highest-impact framing available for an enterprise client and
is worth writing even as a conditional: "this `.p12` is the enrolment certificate for `<realm>`".
items.ruled_out_when:
The recovered data contains no corporate credential, certificate or VPN
configuration — searched with the pattern set above, not by eye.

items.title: Run the pre-severity gate against the Critical claim, not against the primitive
items.severity_note: Support (it governs every Critical and High in this chapter)
items.applies_to: every Critical/High claim in this domain
items.maps_to: the bug-hunting corpus's Pre-Severity Gate and Multi-Tool Reproduction Bar
items.test:
This domain produces more mid-chain primitives than any other — a policy rule, a reachable
service, an exported vendor component, a writable property — and each one *looks* like a device
compromise. Write the draft Critical title, then substitute the Critical claim for "the bug" in five
questions:
1. Have I validated the **full chain** to attacker-attainable impact, or only one primitive in the
   middle? "Policy rule confirmed" is not "escalation demonstrated".
2. What does the attacker walk away with, in one concrete sentence?
3. Have I personally reproduced the full chain end to end **at least twice** — once during discovery,
   once for the PoC?
4. Is there an inheritance gate, signature check, SELinux type or user-id comparison still gating the
   chain? If yes, it is not Critical — document it as "primitive present" at a lower severity.
5. Has the programme rejected this severity class before?
items.how:
For any Critical or High, reproduce through **two independent tools with different stacks** —
`adb shell` plus a PoC APK, or `service call` plus a reflected `IBinder.transact`; the reproduction
commands in the report must be paste-into-shell ready.
```bash
# question 4, mechanised for this domain
sesearch -A -s untrusted_app -t <target_type> -c <class> policy.bin      # is MAC still in the way?
adb shell dumpsys package com.poc.app | sed -n '/requested permissions/,/install permissions/p'
```
items.proof:
Two independent reproductions, and an explicit answer to question 4 quoting the `sesearch`
or `Permission Denial` output that shows nothing is still gating the chain.
items.escalation:
n/a — it is a kill gate. The corpus's own worked failure is instructive: a confirmed
signature-bypass primitive was labelled Critical, a further trust check still rejected it, the chain
never completed, and the finding had to be retracted.
items.ruled_out_when:
All five answers are clean. Then file at the Critical severity and say in the report
that you ran the gate — it reads as rigour, not padding.

items.title: Body-diff, layer-ordering and server-policy-vs-state gates on privileged-surface probes
items.severity_note: Support (it is the false-positive kill gate for D25-020, D25-022 and D25-063)
items.applies_to: every probe in this chapter that reads a status, a Parcel or an HTTP response
items.maps_to: the bug-hunting corpus's Body-Diff Rule, the Layer-Ordering Trap, Server-Policy-vs-State, Marker Discipline and the Statistical-Sample Rule
items.test: Four false positives dominate this domain, and all four look like a bypass.
items.how:
```bash
# 1. BODY DIFF - a byte-identical 200 is not a bypass. Applies to the companion-API diff (D25-063)
diff <(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOK" https://api.target/v2/orders/9001) \
     <(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOK" https://api.target/v1/orders/9001)
wc -c /tmp/baseline /tmp/test     # a 5-byte delta may be a correlation id, not content

# 2. LAYER ORDERING - a validation error does NOT prove you passed auth. Re-test with a minimal {}
curl -s -X POST https://api.target/v1/companion/sync -d '{'
# 400 {"message":"Invalid text. Only permitted characters are allowed"}  <- body parser, not auth
curl -s -X POST https://api.target/v1/companion/sync -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
# 401 {"message":"Not authenticated."}  <- NOW you know where the auth layer sits

# 3. SERVER POLICY vs STATE - the on-device analogue: a provider that denies EVERY uri is a
#    fixed policy, not an oracle. Query a URI you know does not exist and compare.
adb shell content query --uri content://<authority>/definitely-not-a-real-path
adb shell content query --uri content://<authority>/real-path

# 4. MARKER DISCIPLINE - write an 8+ char random marker through the surface, and search the
#    BASELINE for it first. Never use "test", "marker", "AAAA" or a dictionary word.
MARK=$(head -c16 /dev/urandom | base64 | tr -dc 'a-z0-9' | head -c10); echo "$MARK"
adb shell content insert --uri content://<authority>/x --bind note:s:$MARK
adb shell content query  --uri content://<authority>/x | grep -c "$MARK"
```
For any claim about a missing rate limit or a timing difference on a privileged surface: n ≥ 10
interleaved trials per group in randomised order, and require the suspect group's mean to sit at least
2σ from the control's. A single outlier is jitter.
items.proof:
The byte-level diff, the two-request layer-ordering pair, the non-existent-URI control, and
the baseline marker search — whichever apply — present in the report alongside the claim.
items.escalation: n/a — it is a correctness gate on this chapter's HTTP- and Parcel-shaped findings.
items.ruled_out_when:
The bodies are byte-identical, or the well-formed `{}` request returns the auth
error while only the malformed one returned a parser error. Write the retraction into the appendix with
the disproving evidence rather than silently dropping the claim.

items.title: Chain-filing order, evidence hygiene and retraction discipline for a device chain
items.severity_note: Support
items.applies_to: every multi-finding device or OEM engagement
items.maps_to: the bug-hunting corpus's chain-filing order, five-screenshot pattern, PII mask/leave-visible split, and retraction discipline
items.test:
Device chains are long — a policy rule, an exported component, a file write, an install — and
each link usually has its own fix surface and therefore its own bounty. Filing the chain as one report
costs you money; filing each link as a Critical costs you credibility.
items.how:
(1) Identify the highest-severity chained outcome. (2) File each primitive as a separate report
at its **standalone** severity — typically P3/P4 — with a placeholder cross-reference line. (3) File the
chain consumer with the full narrative at the chained severity, filling in the real primitive ids.
(4) Edit each primitive to backfill the consumer's id.
```markdown
## Chain partners (filed as separate reports)
- **submission [UUID-1]** - exported vendor receiver accepting SAVE_PATH (primitive)
- **submission [UUID-2]** - privapp-permissions enforcement set to `log` (primitive)
These primitives have independent fix surfaces and are filed separately per the programme's
"one fix = one bounty" rule.
```
Do **not** paste the whole chain narrative into every primitive, claim each primitive is independently
P1, or ask for a single combined bounty — frame the chain as a *severity amplifier*, not a merge
request. Order of submission: primitives → consumer → clean standalone findings → scope-risky findings
last. Never file everything in one batch within minutes; triagers read that as low-effort spam.
**Evidence:** use the five-screenshot state-change pattern — pre-state, the bug firing, the negative
post-state (what it looks like without the attack), the positive post-state, and the side effect. Mask
victim PII; **leave visible** the trace ids, your own attacker uid, the package names, the SELinux
contexts and the JSON key names — the triager needs those to reproduce.
items.proof:
Cross-referenced ids in both directions, and an evidence bundle whose masking has not
destroyed the reproduction path.
items.escalation: Two payouts instead of one.
items.ruled_out_when:
There is a single finding with a single fix surface. **Do not retract a confirmed
finding that stopped reproducing** — assume the client patched mid-engagement, and keep the timestamped
pre-patch evidence. Retract only what you disproved, and do it in an appendix with the disproving
evidence attached.

items.title: Never instrument production hardware; record the root path you used
items.severity_note: Support
items.applies_to: test devices only; never on client-owned production hardware without written authorisation
items.maps_to: the bug-hunting corpus's operational boundary; drozer `tools.setup.minimalsu`, `tools.setup.toybox`, `shell.exec`, `shell.start`, `shell.send`, `clean`
items.test:
A rooted device changes the validity of every resilience claim and most device claims. Obtain
root explicitly and reversibly, record that you did, and state it next to every root-dependent finding.
items.how:
```
dz> run tools.setup.minimalsu
dz> run tools.setup.toybox
dz> run shell.exec "id"
dz> run shell.start
dz> clean
```
`tools.setup.minimalsu` "prepares 'minimal-su' binary installation on the device" — it uploads
`minimal-su` and `install-minimal-su.sh`, `chmod 770`s the script, and instructs you to execute it
*from root context*. It **does not gain root for you**; it stages `su` for use after a root exploit.
`clean` removes drozer's temporary device files.
items.proof:
`run shell.exec "id"` output showing the UID you were operating as, recorded next to every
root-dependent finding so the reader can judge realism.
items.escalation:
Enables `--privileged` scanner runs and `/data` inspection — and nothing else. Any
finding that required root must say so; one that requires root **and** has no non-root path is usually
Low unless the app's own threat model claims to defend rooted devices.
items.ruled_out_when:
n/a — it is a rule, not a test. The only acceptable output is the recorded UID and
the `clean` confirmation.

items.title: The target, or an OEM preload, holds UICC carrier privileges — a privileged class the permission tables miss
items.severity_note: Support for the determination; High when an exported component re-delegates a carrier-privileged call
items.applies_to: packages whose signing certificate is in the SIM's ARA-M access rules or in `carrier_config` `carrier_certificate_string_array`; carrier, MVNO and OEM telephony apps
items.maps_to: MASTG-KNOW-0017; AOSP "UICC Carrier Privileges" documentation; `TelephonyManager.hasCarrierPrivileges()` / `getCarrierPrivilegeStatus()`
items.record: `logs/D25-080.txt` (the tracker and carrier_config dumps, the SIM MCC/MNC); `pocs/F-NNN/` for a re-delegated call
items.skip_when: no SIM is inserted in any held device (`adb -s "$SERIAL" shell getprop gsm.sim.state` prints only `ABSENT` / `NOT_READY`) — write `D25-080 blocked: no SIM`, not n/a, because the privileges are granted per inserted SIM.
items.test: Carrier privileges grant identifier reads (IMEI/IMSI), `iccOpenLogicalChannel`/`iccTransmitApdu`, `setLine1NumberForDisplay`, carrier-config overrides and network-selection control with no manifest permission and no runtime prompt. They are granted per inserted SIM and never appear as `granted=true`, so every permission sweep in this chapter misses them. A holder is a privileged package by another route and its exported surface re-rates like D25-009.
items.how:
```bash
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys phone | grep -iA6 -e 'CarrierPrivilegesTracker' -e 'UiccCarrierPrivilegeRules'   # privileged packages per subscription (the tracker on 13+, the UICC rules dump before)
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys carrier_config | grep -iE 'carrier_certificate|privileged'
grep -rnE 'hasCarrierPrivileges|getCarrierPrivilegeStatus|iccOpenLogicalChannel|iccTransmitApdu|setLine1NumberForDisplay|CarrierConfigManager' $DEC/jadx/sources | head
# hasCarrierPrivileges() answers only for the calling app and getCarrierPrivilegeStatus(uid) is a SystemApi: a zero-permission
# probe cannot census other packages — the dumps above are the census; the probe is for exercising a holder's exported component
```
items.proof: `CarrierPrivilegesTracker` naming the package for the active subscription (or `hasCarrierPrivileges()==true` in its own log), plus an exported component of that package returning a restricted identifier or performing a call/SMS/APDU action for the zero-permission PoC.

items.title: A preload's effective capability is permissions + app-ops + roles + pre-enabled services — census all four
items.severity_note: Support; High when a pre-granted op, role or listener is reachable through an exported component
items.applies_to: OEM/carrier images; the target where it is preloaded
items.maps_to: MASTG-KNOW-0017; Android `AppOpsManager` / `RoleManager` documentation; D03-022 for role mechanics; MASTG-DEMO-0104 (`SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW`)
items.record: `logs/D25-081.txt` (the four dumps and the counted app-ops sweep); `inventory/oem-capabilities.csv`: `package \| grant table \| capability \| exported component that re-delegates it`
items.skip_when: the Applicability probe excluded the OEM block (store build only, target not preinstalled) — write the partial-n/a note; on an OEM scope this item always runs.
items.test: `granted=true` (D25-009) is one of four grant tables. OEM images pre-allow app-ops (`PROJECT_MEDIA`, `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW`, `GET_USAGE_STATS`, `ACCESS_RESTRICTED_SETTINGS`), pre-hold roles (gallery, dialer, SMS, assistant, wallet, notes) and pre-enable accessibility, notification-listener and device-admin components for vendor packages with no prompt; each is a capability, and an exported component in the holder re-delegates it to a zero-permission caller (the factory/diagnostic-preload shape).
items.how:
```bash
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys role | grep -iE 'name=|role\.|holders' | head -80     # holders per role (or: cmd role get-role-holders <role>)
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell settings get secure enabled_accessibility_services
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell settings get secure enabled_notification_listeners
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell 'dpm list-owners; dumpsys device_policy | grep -A3 Admin'
python3 - <<'PY'     # app-ops per OEM-only package, counted (D25-006)
import subprocess
S='<serial>'; pk=[l.strip() for l in open('oem-only-pkgs.txt') if l.strip()]; print('input',len(pk)); hits=[]
OPS=('PROJECT_MEDIA','SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW','GET_USAGE_STATS','ACCESS_RESTRICTED_SETTINGS','MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE','RECORD_AUDIO','CAMERA','ACCESS_ACCESSIBILITY')
for p in pk:
    o=subprocess.run(['adb','-s',S,'shell','appops','get',p],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout
    bad=[l.strip() for l in o.splitlines() if ':' in l and l.split(':')[0].strip() in OPS and l.split(':',1)[1].split(';')[0].strip()=='allow']   # line = "OP: mode; time=…"
    if bad: hits.append((p,bad)); print('OP',p,bad)
print('probed',len(pk),'hits',len(hits))
PY
```
items.proof: The op/role/listener line naming the package, plus the effect reached from the zero-permission PoC through that package's exported surface — a screen capture started under `PROJECT_MEDIA`, a notification body returned, an accessibility action performed.
items.escalation: → D25-009 tiers; → D25-021 when the holder is a factory/diag package; → D20 for what a listener reads; → D04 overlay items for `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW`.
items.ruled_out_when: every pre-allowed op, role holder and enabled listener belongs to a package whose components are all guarded by signature permissions (verified from the PoC, D25-017), and `appops get` over the OEM-only set shows only `default`/`ignore` for the listed ops — with `probed == input`.

items.title: Enterprise provisioning payload (QR / NFC bump / zero-touch): weak DPC binding or a reusable enrolment secret
items.severity_note: High (a rogue device enrolled into the fleet, or a downgraded DPC on a fleet device); Critical only if a device installs a substituted DPC from an unpinned download
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.for_internal_asset` (**P3**) for a reusable enrolment token or PSK; `insecure_os_firmware.weakness_in_firmware_updates.firmware_does_not_validate_update_integrity` (**P3**, argue up) for an unbound or downgradable DPC download
items.attacker: AM-06 network attacker during enrolment; AM-11 physical at a factory-reset device, holding a copy of the payload (QR codes are routinely printed or posted)
items.applies_to: fleets provisioned by QR, NFC bump or zero-touch; the client's DPC
items.maps_to: Android `DevicePolicyManager` `EXTRA_PROVISIONING_DEVICE_ADMIN_PACKAGE_DOWNLOAD_LOCATION` / `_PACKAGE_CHECKSUM` / `_SIGNATURE_CHECKSUM`, `EXTRA_PROVISIONING_ADMIN_EXTRAS_BUNDLE`, `EXTRA_PROVISIONING_WIFI_PASSWORD`; the Android Enterprise provisioning guide
items.record: `logs/D25-083.txt` (the decoded payload, redacted of the Wi-Fi PSK and the token); `pocs/F-NNN/` with the enrolment transcript
items.skip_when: the client provisions no device (no QR, NFC or zero-touch payload exists; BYOD work profile only) — write `D25-083 n/a: no provisioning payload in scope`.
items.test: The payload names where the DPC is downloaded from and how it is verified, and usually carries secrets. Current ManagedProvisioning refuses a download location that has neither `…_PACKAGE_CHECKSUM` nor `…_SIGNATURE_CHECKSUM` — confirm that on the test unit instead of assuming it, because a device that provisions from an unpinned download hands device owner to whoever serves the APK (the Critical). The realistic defects are weaker and common: (1) `SIGNATURE_CHECKSUM` alone pins the signer, not the build, so an `http://` or attacker-reachable download location can serve an **older, vulnerable** DPC signed by the same key; (2) the enrolment token in `…_ADMIN_EXTRAS_BUNDLE` is reusable, unexpiring or not device-bound, so anyone holding the payload enrols a rogue device and receives the fleet's managed configuration; (3) the enrolment Wi-Fi PSK travels in the clear inside the payload.
items.how:
```bash
zbarimg -q --raw enrol.png | jq .      # or decode the NFC NDEF record / the zero-touch configuration JSON
# inspect: android.app.extra.PROVISIONING_DEVICE_ADMIN_PACKAGE_DOWNLOAD_LOCATION (scheme, host),
#   PROVISIONING_DEVICE_ADMIN_PACKAGE_CHECKSUM (pins the file) vs PROVISIONING_DEVICE_ADMIN_SIGNATURE_CHECKSUM (pins only the signer),
#   PROVISIONING_ADMIN_EXTRAS_BUNDLE (the enrolment token: single-use? expiry? device-bound?), PROVISIONING_WIFI_PASSWORD,
#   PROVISIONING_SKIP_ENCRYPTION, PROVISIONING_LEAVE_ALL_SYSTEM_APPS_ENABLED
grep -rnE 'PROVISIONING_DEVICE_ADMIN_(PACKAGE|SIGNATURE)_CHECKSUM|DOWNLOAD_LOCATION|ADMIN_EXTRAS_BUNDLE' $DEC/jadx/sources provisioning-docs/
# on a factory-reset test unit, with the client's written permission: enrol a second unit with the same payload (token reuse);
# where only the signer is pinned, serve an older signed DPC build from the download location (downgrade)
adb -s "$SERIAL" logcat -d | grep -iE 'ManagedProvisioning|checksum|DownloadPackage|VerifyPackage'
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dpm list-owners
```
items.proof: The decoded payload showing the weakness, plus one of: a second unit enrolled with the same token and receiving the managed configuration (`dpm list-owners` naming the DPC on both); an older DPC build installed from your host under a signature-only pin (`dumpsys package <dpc> | grep versionName`); or — the Critical — a unit provisioning from an unpinned download, with the logcat.
items.escalation: device owner = every policy in D25-068..073 is the attacker's; → D25-075 enterprise pivot; the Wi-Fi PSK in the payload → D14 (a network position on the enrolment SSID).
items.ruled_out_when: the payload pins the file with `…_PACKAGE_CHECKSUM` (or the unit refuses an unpinned or substituted download — the ManagedProvisioning checksum failure in logcat), the download URL is https on a client-controlled host, and the second enrolment with the same token is refused — quote the refusal.
